passage: Every evening at 8:30, Noor sat at the small table by the window of her Pune flat, set a timer on her phone for fifteen minutes and opened a green notebook. Tonight the list ran fast: the rent going up, her father's knee, a vague line her manager Thomas had written in the review, the scooter's odd rattle. When the timer was half done she drew a tick beside the two she could do something about. She wrote one small step next to the review line: "Ask Thomas for a ten-minute call on Friday." Beside her father's knee she wrote, "Not mine to fix tonight. Tomorrow's slot." At the beep she closed the notebook. At 10:40, lying awake, the knee came back to her. She whispered, "8:30 tomorrow," and turned over.

qa.q: What did Noor write next to the review line?
qa.a: She wrote, "Ask Thomas for a ten-minute call on Friday."

qa.q: Why does closing the notebook at the beep make sense to Noor, even though her worries are not solved?
qa.a: She has already turned the useful worries into a next step, so going over them again would only be spinning. Saying "8:30 tomorrow" lets her trust that the rest has a place to go.

qa.q: At 10:40 the knee worry came back. What choice did Noor make then, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She chose to send it back to tomorrow's slot instead of starting to think it through in bed. That kept the worry from taking over her night.

qa.q: How might Thomas experience the Friday call Noor is planning?
qa.a: Thomas gets a clear, short question about the review line instead of a tense or silent team member, and may be glad of the chance to explain what the line meant.

grounding: It shows an adult keeping a timed worry slot, ticking the worries she can act on, taking one step and sending the rest back to the slot.

passage:
"Kishore, it's midnight. You're scrolling again."
"I can't sleep, Gurleen. The loan, the car service, your mum's visit, the audit..."
"Remember what we tried last month? Write it down. Fifteen minutes. I'll time it."
"Now?"
"Tomorrow, after dinner. Tonight you just tell it: 'not now, seven o'clock.'"
Next evening Gurleen set the kitchen timer. Kishore filled half a page.
"Okay. Circle the ones you can do anything about this week."
"The car service. I can book it. The audit... I can ask Rao for the checklist."
"And the loan?"
"The rate is not up to me." He laughed a little. "It stays on the list."
"Pick one."
He booked the car service right there on his phone.
"Done. That felt ridiculous and good." 🙂
"Same time tomorrow," said Gurleen, taking the timer back.

qa.q: What did Kishore book on his phone during the fifteen minutes?
qa.a: He booked the car service right there on his phone.

qa.q: What does Kishore's line "That felt ridiculous and good" suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels a bit silly for how simple the step was, but also relieved. Acting on one worry gave him a sense of control the midnight scrolling never did.

qa.q: When the worry came at midnight, Gurleen did not let Kishore sort it out then. Why was that turn in the conversation useful?
qa.a: Gurleen moved the worrying to a set time the next evening, so the night was not spent spinning. The next day, with a timer, he could sort the worries and act on one.

qa.q: How is Gurleen affected by Kishore's midnight worrying, and why might Gurleen want this routine too?
qa.a: Kishore's scrolling keeps them both awake and tense. A fixed worry time gives Gurleen calmer nights and a way to help that does not mean arguing at midnight.

grounding: Gurleen helps Kishore use a timed worry slot: he lists worries, circles the ones he can act on, does one, and leaves the loan rate on the list.

passage: I'm Samir, and last winter I was the man who worried in the shower, on the bus and at 3 a.m. My flatmate Francis suggested something that sounded too neat to work. He said, "Give worry an appointment." So I did. Seven p.m., the kitchen, a cheap notebook, fifteen minutes on the microwave timer. I wrote everything: my visa papers, my sister's exam, a cough that wouldn't go. Then I split the page. Left side, things I could move. Right side, things I couldn't. The visa form went left, and I filled it in that night. My sister's exam went right. Some days the right side was longer, and that stung. But when a worry showed up at work, I'd tell myself, "Seven o'clock," and most days it actually waited. Francis still teases me about the microwave.

qa.q: Where and when did Samir keep his worry appointment?
qa.a: Seven p.m., in the kitchen, with a cheap notebook and fifteen minutes on the microwave timer.

qa.q: Why did it sting Samir when the right side of the page was longer?
qa.a: It meant many of his worries were things he could not change, which is hard to accept. He still kept those worries on the page rather than turning them over all day.

qa.q: Which step turned the list from a page of fears into something useful for Samir?
qa.a: Splitting the page into things he could move and things he couldn't, then acting on one, like filling in the visa form that night.

qa.q: How might Francis have seen Samir before and after the appointment idea?
qa.a: Before, Francis lived with a flatmate who was worried and distracted at all hours. After, he sees Samir calmer and can joke about the microwave, which shows the change was real.

grounding: A young adult keeps a timed evening worry slot, sorts worries into those he can and cannot act on, acts on one and lets the others wait.

passage: The lemon-and-spoon race at the Bhatpara fair was over in a minute. Sharmila's lemon rolled into the dust just before the line, and three girls ran past her. She stood still, then burst into loud, angry tears. Her aunt Minakshi pushed through the crowd and knelt beside her. She didn't say "don't cry." She held Sharmila's dusty hands and said, "You were so fast. That's why it hurts so much." Sharmila cried into her aunt's shoulder until her breathing slowed. They shared a paper cone of roasted chana. When the teacher called for the second heat, Sharmila looked up. "Can I go again?" Minakshi wiped her face with the end of her dupatta. "Hold the spoon a little lower this time." Sharmila ran. She finished fourth, grinning.

qa.q: What happened to Sharmila's lemon in the first race?
qa.a: It rolled into the dust just before the line, and three girls ran past her.

qa.q: Why do you think Sharmila felt ready to ask "Can I go again?"
qa.a: Her aunt had stayed close, let her cry and told her the hurt made sense, so the loss no longer felt too big. Feeling safe gave her the courage to try.

qa.q: Minakshi could have told Sharmila to stop crying. What did she choose instead, and why did it help?
qa.a: She knelt, held her hands and said the hurt made sense because Sharmila had been so fast. Being understood calmed Sharmila faster than being told to stop.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt when Sharmila finished fourth, grinning?
qa.a: She was probably proud and relieved, because the girl who had been crying in the dust was now happy to have tried again. 😊

grounding: A girl who loses a race cries, is comforted by her aunt, and then runs the second heat with a grin.

passage: In their flat in Valencia, Tomas lost at chess to his big brother Mateo for the sixth time that week. His king was trapped in the corner. Tomas swept the pieces off the board and ran to the balcony, crying hard. Mateo followed. He didn't laugh. He sat on the cold tiles next to his brother and waited. After a while he said, "When I was nine, I threw the whole board at Papá." Tomas sniffed. "Really?" "Really. Losing feels awful. You're allowed to be mad." They watched the scooters below for a bit. Then Mateo said, "Want me to show you how I trapped your king?" Tomas nodded. They picked up the pieces together. The next game lasted twice as long, and Tomas took Mateo's queen.

qa.q: Where did Tomas run after sweeping the pieces off the board?
qa.a: He ran to the balcony, crying hard.

qa.q: What did Tomas probably feel when Mateo said he once threw the whole board at Papá?
qa.a: He likely felt less ashamed and less alone, because even his big brother had felt that angry. His "Really?" shows he was surprised and starting to calm.

qa.q: What was the turning point that got Tomas back to the board?
qa.a: Mateo sat with him without laughing and said losing feels awful, then offered to show him the trap. Being accepted first made him willing to learn.

qa.q: What is it like for Mateo to keep beating his younger brother?
qa.a: He may feel a little guilty or unsure how to help. Sitting on the balcony and sharing his own story lets him be a brother instead of just the winner.

grounding: A boy who loses at chess cries on the balcony, his older brother comforts him, and he plays again.

passage: At the Saturday badminton club in the community centre, Santosh, ten, lost his first match 21–6. He walked off the court, sat against the wall and pulled his cap down, shoulders shaking. Coach Hansa finished calling scores, then sat on the floor next to him in silence. "That was a tough one," she said quietly. Santosh wiped his nose on his wrist. "I'm the worst." "You're upset. Of course you are. You wanted it." She gave him her water bottle. "I lost a lot at your age. I cried in the changing room every week." He peeked from under the cap. "Every week?" "Nearly." Then she said, "Court three's free. Want to hit some drops with me?" He stood up. They rallied until the lights clicked off.

qa.q: What was the score of Santosh's first match?
qa.a: He lost his first match 21–6.

qa.q: What does Santosh's cap pulled down suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He was ashamed and did not want others to see him crying. He felt like "the worst" after the loss.

qa.q: Coach Hansa sat with Santosh before suggesting more play. Why was that timing a good choice?
qa.a: If she had pushed him back on court at once, he might have felt his tears did not matter. Waiting and naming his feelings first made trying again feel safe.

qa.q: How might the other children at the club see Coach Hansa after this?
qa.a: They may see her as someone who stays with you when you lose, not only when you win. That can make them less afraid of losing in front of her.

grounding: A boy who loses a badminton match cries, is comforted by his coach, and goes back to practise with her.

passage: The list went up at 3:55, five minutes before the school bus left. Binita's name wasn't on the debate team. She had practised for three weeks. On the crowded bus, wedged between bags, Divyansh leaned over. "Were you on it?" Her automatic answer was ready: "It's fine, I didn't even care." Instead, with the engine roaring and a Class 6 kid kicking her seat, she heard herself say, "No. I'm really disappointed. And kind of embarrassed, because I told everyone I'd get in." Divyansh nodded. "Yeah. That's rough." That was all. No pep talk, no fuss. Binita stared out at the traffic for two stops. By the fourth stop she was arguing with him about a cricket score. At home she told her mother the same words, and it came out easier the second time.

qa.q: How long had Binita practised for the debate team?
qa.a: She had practised for three weeks.

qa.q: Why might Binita have been tempted to say "It's fine, I didn't even care"?
qa.a: Saying she was fine would have protected her pride, especially since she had told everyone she'd get in. Admitting the hurt felt riskier in front of a friend.

qa.q: On the crowded bus Binita had a choice between hiding and naming what she felt. What did the choice change?
qa.a: Naming disappointment and embarrassment let the feeling pass in a couple of stops, and she was soon arguing about cricket. It was also easier to tell her mother later.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel when Binita answered honestly instead of brushing off the question?
qa.a: Divyansh probably felt trusted, and it was easy to respond simply with "That's rough." A pretend "fine" would have left Divyansh unsure what to say.

grounding: A teenager on a crowded bus names her disappointment and embarrassment about missing the debate team instead of saying she is fine, and moves through it quickly.

passage: Madhuri came out of the music school in Andheri with her violin case held tight. She had stopped twice in the middle of the exam piece and started over. Gurpreet, her friend from the building, was waiting on the steps with two cutting chais from the stall. "So?" she asked. Madhuri opened her mouth to say "fine." It stuck. "Actually... I'm gutted. And embarrassed. The examiner was so polite about it, which was worse." Gurpreet handed her a chai. "Gutted and embarrassed. Got it." Madhuri laughed, a wobbly laugh. "Saying it makes it smaller, somehow." They walked towards the station. By the signal Madhuri was already thinking about which bars had tripped her. "I'll ask Ma'am about bar forty on Monday," she said.

qa.q: How many times did Madhuri stop during the exam piece?
qa.a: She stopped twice in the middle of the exam piece and started over.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri say the examiner being polite was worse?
qa.a: The politeness made her feel pitied, which added to her embarrassment. She felt that everyone had noticed her mistakes.

qa.q: What was the moment that let Madhuri move from the bad exam to planning her next step?
qa.a: When she dropped "fine" and said she was gutted and embarrassed, the feeling shrank enough that by the signal she was thinking about bar forty.

qa.q: If you were Gurpreet, why might you be glad Madhuri didn't just say "fine"?
qa.a: Her honest answer lets Gurpreet actually support her with a chai and a repeat of her words. A "fine" would have kept Gurpreet guessing and at arm's length.

grounding: A teenager leaving a music exam names being gutted and embarrassed to her friend, and then quickly starts planning.

passage:
"Nilesh? You've been in the bathroom for twenty minutes."
"I'm fine, bhaiya."
Tarun leaned on the door. "You said the results were out."
Silence. Then the lock clicked. Nilesh came out, eyes red.
"I got 54 in maths. I told Aai I'd get 80."
"Okay. How are you feeling about it?"
"Fine. I said. Whatever."
Tarun waited.
"...Not fine. Disappointed. And embarrassed, because I bragged at dinner."
"That makes sense. I'd feel both."
Nilesh sat on the stairs. "Weird. That's better. Just saying it."
"Want to tell Aai together?"
"Give me five minutes."
Five minutes later, he walked into the kitchen himself. "Aai, the result's bad. I'm disappointed."
Aai put the ladle down. "Come, sit. Show me the paper."

qa.q: What mark did Nilesh get in maths?
qa.a: He got 54 in maths.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh hide in the bathroom and keep saying "Fine"?
qa.a: He felt ashamed because he had bragged at dinner that he would get 80. Pretending to be fine felt safer than admitting that.

qa.q: What choice did Nilesh make after sitting on the stairs, and why was it a turning point?
qa.a: He chose to walk into the kitchen himself and tell Aai plainly that he was disappointed. Having named the feeling once, he could face her without hiding.

qa.q: What would have changed if Tarun had accepted "I'm fine" and walked away?
qa.a: Nilesh might have stayed locked in with his shame much longer, and Aai might have found out in a harder way. Tarun's waiting gave him room to be honest.

grounding: A teenage boy stops saying he is fine and names being disappointed and embarrassed to his older brother, then tells his mother.

passage:
Wednesday, late
Diary, I did it. I told Arohi.
For weeks I've been waking at 4 and just lying there. School feels like wading through mud, and I stopped going to the terrace with the others. I kept telling everyone "just tired." Today Arohi (my cousin, the one who calls me "Hansu") stayed over, and while we were brushing our teeth she said, "You're not okay, na?" I nearly said "I'm fine." Then I started crying with toothpaste on my chin.
She didn't freak out. She sat on the edge of the bath and listened. She said, "Let's tell Mummy now. I'll come with you." I said yes.
Mummy turned off the TV and held my hand while I talked. She said it wasn't my fault, and that we'll talk to the school counsellor together.
I don't feel fixed. But I feel less alone than I have in a month.
Hansa

qa.q: Whom did Hansa tell, and where were they when it happened?
qa.a: Hansa told cousin Arohi, while they were brushing their teeth.

qa.q: What does "less alone than I have in a month" suggest about Hansa?
qa.a: Hansa had been carrying the low mood alone for weeks, and telling Arohi eased that loneliness even though the problem is not solved.

qa.q: Hansa nearly said "I'm fine" again. Why was saying yes to telling Mummy that same night an important choice?
qa.a: Arohi's support is real, but a parent can do more, and Mummy's calm answer led straight to a plan to see the school counsellor together.

qa.q: How might Arohi have been feeling when she asked "You're not okay, na?"
qa.a: She had probably noticed Hansa pulling away and was worried. Asking was a risk, and staying calm when Hansa cried shows she cared more about Hansa than about saying the perfect thing.

grounding: A teenager who has been struggling for weeks tells a cousin instead of hiding it, and that night they tell Mummy, who listens and plans help together.

passage: In Kotpur the bus to the higher secondary school left at 6:15, and for a month Divyansh had been missing it on purpose. His father's tea stall had been shut since the flood, money was tight, and Divyansh had started doing the morning milk round for a dairy instead. He told no one at school. On Thursday, Mohit Sir found him at the bus stand in the evening, sitting on his cycle. "Haven't seen you in class, Divyansh." Divyansh shrugged, ready to say "sick." Then, looking at the teacher's worried face, he told it all: the stall, the milk round, how he lay awake doing sums. Mohit Sir listened to the end. "Thank you for telling me. Let's talk to your father together, and I'll ask about the scholarship form." Divyansh cycled home feeling lighter.

qa.q: Why had the tea stall been shut?
qa.a: It had been shut since the flood.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh keep his problems from everyone at school?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed about the money trouble and thought he had to handle it himself. Saying "sick" was easier than explaining.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Divyansh, and what did it open up?
qa.a: Choosing to tell Mohit Sir the truth instead of "sick." That brought in an adult who could speak to his father and look into a scholarship form.

qa.q: How might Mohit Sir have felt while he waited at the bus stand for an answer?
qa.a: He was worried about a student who had vanished from class. Hearing the real reason may have made him sad for Divyansh but glad to finally be able to help.

grounding: A teenager in a small town tells his teacher about his family's money trouble instead of hiding it, and gets support.

passage:
Monday. Lakshmi checked the result at the hostel gate: she had failed Organic Chemistry. She went back to her room and cried into her pillow. Her roommate Sangeeta brought her a steel tumbler of filter coffee and sat on the other bed. "It's awful," Lakshmi said. "I really thought I'd pass." "It is awful," Sangeeta said.
Thursday. Lakshmi opened the old paper with a pencil. She was still sore about it. But she asked herself a new question: what does this show about how I studied? The pattern was plain. She had read notes but never practised mechanisms by hand, and she'd crammed the last two nights.
Two weeks later. A timetable was taped above her desk: one mechanism a day, written out, checked by Sangeeta on Fridays. "Resit's in July," Lakshmi said. "I think I can actually pass it now."

qa.q: Which paper did Lakshmi fail?
qa.a: She had failed Organic Chemistry.

qa.q: On Thursday, how did Lakshmi feel while reading the old paper?
qa.a: She was still sore about failing, so the disappointment had not vanished. But she was curious enough to look for what the paper could teach her.

qa.q: What was the key turn between Monday and two weeks later?
qa.a: Lakshmi let herself be upset first, then asked what the failure showed about her study method. That question led to the daily mechanism timetable.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta see Lakshmi's change over the two weeks?
qa.a: Sangeeta watched Lakshmi go from crying into a pillow to building a plan Sangeeta could help check. That probably feels useful and hopeful for July.

grounding: A student who failed a paper first feels the disappointment, then asks what it reveals about her preparation, and builds a new study plan.

passage: Shankar, sit. You've been staring at that result on your phone all evening. Let me tell you about 1978. I'm Madhav, your grandfather, and I failed Engineering Drawing in my second year. Failed it badly. I remember walking home by the canal, so angry I kicked a stone into the water. I told nobody for two days. Then my friend Iqbal asked me straight: "So what went wrong?" I wanted to say "the examiner." But I made myself answer honestly. I had skipped the drawing hall and copied sheets from the seniors. I didn't know my own set squares. That hurt more than the mark. So I asked the lab assistant if I could use the hall on Sundays. The next year I got a first in that same subject. Be sad tonight, beta. Tomorrow, ask what it's telling you.

qa.q: Which subject did Madhav fail in his second year?
qa.a: He failed Engineering Drawing in his second year.

qa.q: Why did it hurt Madhav more to realise he had copied sheets than to see the mark?
qa.a: The honest answer showed that the failure was partly his own doing, which is harder to face than blaming the examiner. It also showed him exactly what he had to change.

qa.q: What choice after Iqbal's question changed things for Madhav?
qa.a: He chose to answer honestly instead of blaming the examiner, then asked to use the drawing hall on Sundays. That turned a bad mark into a plan.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel hearing that Shankar's grandfather once kicked a stone into the canal over a result?
qa.a: Shankar may feel less ashamed of the disappointment and more able to face it, because someone Shankar respects went through the same thing.

grounding: A grandfather tells a grandchild how he admitted his disappointment after failing a paper and then asked what it showed about his preparation.

passage: Manjula found out she had failed Statistics fifteen minutes before her shift at the bakery. There was no time to cry properly, and no quiet place either: the ovens roared and orders piled up. Between trays, she let herself feel it. "I failed," she muttered to the dough. "That really hurts." Her co-worker Shreya glanced over. "Exam?" "Stats. I'm gutted." Shreya slid her a cooling rusk. At the break, sitting on a flour sack with her phone, Manjula made herself look at the marks breakdown. The theory answers were fine. She'd lost almost everything in the problem section, where she'd rushed. So it wasn't "I'm bad at this." It was "I never practised timed problems." She typed a note: "Two past papers a week, timed, on days off." Then the bell rang and she went back to the ovens.

qa.q: How long before her shift did Manjula find out she had failed Statistics?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes before her shift at the bakery.

qa.q: Why did Manjula mutter "That really hurts" to the dough?
qa.a: She had no time or quiet place to cry, so naming it under her breath let her admit the disappointment instead of pushing it away.

qa.q: What did Manjula notice in the marks breakdown, and how did it change her plan?
qa.a: She saw she had lost almost everything in the problem section where she rushed. That turned "I'm bad at this" into a concrete plan of timed past papers.

qa.q: How might Shreya see Manjula during that shift?
qa.a: Shreya can tell Manjula is hurting but still working, and a quiet rusk is a way to show care without making a scene in the busy bakery.

grounding: A student who failed Statistics admits the disappointment during a busy shift, then reads the marks to see what went wrong with her preparation.

passage:
"Chinmay, it's eleven. You haven't eaten."
"I'm not hungry, Thomas. The placement test is in nine days."
"You said that yesterday. Dal's still warm. Five minutes."
"...Fine."
Chinmay ate standing up. Thomas, his cousin, leaned on the fridge.
"Tomorrow, walk with me to the vegetable market at seven."
"I need to study."
"Twenty minutes. You'll study better. You've been rereading one page for an hour."
Next morning, grumbling, Chinmay went. The day after, he went without being asked.
On the sixth night, he shut the laptop at 11:30. "I still don't feel like doing anything, you know. But I'm sleeping."
"That's the point."
"If it doesn't get better after the test, I'll see the college counsellor."
"I'll come with you if you want."

qa.q: Where did Thomas ask Chinmay to walk at seven?
qa.a: To the vegetable market.

qa.q: What does "I still don't feel like doing anything" tell us about Chinmay?
qa.a: He is still stressed and low on motivation. He keeps the routine anyway, which shows he is choosing it rather than waiting to feel ready.

qa.q: On which day did Chinmay start going on the walk without being asked, and why does that choice matter?
qa.a: The day after his first grumbling walk. Choosing it for himself shows the routine was becoming his own, not something Thomas pushed on him.

qa.q: How might Thomas feel when Chinmay mentions the college counsellor?
qa.a: Thomas would likely be relieved that Chinmay knows when to get more help. Offering to go along shows Thomas wants to support Chinmay without carrying it all alone.

grounding: A young man under exam stress keeps meals, sleep and a daily walk going with his cousin's help, and plans to see a counsellor if it does not improve.

passage: My name's Yogesh, and the month my father was in hospital I learned something small. I was a nineteen-year-old boy in second-year B.Com, travelling between the ward and college, and everything felt grey. I didn't want to cook, sleep or do anything. My friend Dhruv didn't give me advice. He just texted every night at ten: "Lights off in thirty?" So I made three rules I could keep even on bad days. Eat something real at lunch, even canteen poha. Walk from the station instead of taking the auto. Lights off by 11. Some nights I lay awake anyway. But the days stopped blurring. I could sit with Papa and actually listen. Once, when I felt heavy for weeks, I did go to the college counsellor, and I'm glad I did. The rules didn't fix everything. They gave me a floor to stand on.

qa.q: What were Yogesh's three rules?
qa.a: Eat something real at lunch, walk from the station instead of taking the auto, and lights off by 11.

qa.q: What does Yogesh mean when he says the rules gave him "a floor to stand on"?
qa.a: He felt that even when everything was grey, the basic routine kept him steady. It did not remove the sadness, but it stopped him from sinking further.

qa.q: When the heaviness lasted for weeks, what choice did Yogesh make, and why was it wise?
qa.a: He went to the college counsellor. Routines help, but lasting distress needs someone qualified, and he did not try to push through alone.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have felt sending the same text every night?
qa.a: Dhruv probably felt a bit helpless about Yogesh's father, so a simple nightly text was a way to care without prying. Seeing Yogesh steadier would have been reassuring.

grounding: A young man with a sick father keeps simple rules about meals, walking and sleep, and sees a counsellor when heaviness lasts.

passage:
Warden's note, Block C, 14 March
I've noticed Chaitanya (Room 212) looking drained since the internship rejection last week. He was skipping mess dinner, and his light was on at 3 a.m. two nights running. I didn't lecture. On Tuesday I asked if he'd join the 6:30 walk round the ground that a few of us do. He came, silent, hands in pockets. Wednesday he came again. By Friday he'd started eating at the mess and said, "I'm still low, sir, but I'm sleeping by midnight." I told him that keeping his basics going on flat days was a real skill, and that if the low mood stays or gets heavier, the campus counsellor and doctor are there, and I'll walk over with him. He nodded. I'll keep checking in quietly.
Lalit, Warden

qa.q: What time was Chaitanya's light on two nights running?
qa.a: His light was on at 3 a.m. two nights running.

subtype: Problem solving one piece at a time [Response]
passage:
Day one. The email said Keerthana's role was "no longer required" from the end of the month. She sat in her car in the office basement for forty minutes, heart racing, thinking about rent, her EMI, her mother's medicines, what she'd tell people. Everything felt like one giant wall.
Day three. Her friend Sahil came over with idli and a notepad. "Write every task. Not feelings, tasks." The list had eleven items. "Which one takes under an hour?" She pointed at "update CV." She did it that night, badly, but did it.
Day nine. The list had five ticks. She'd called HR about her notice pay, messaged two old managers, and signed up for one online course. The fear hadn't gone. But when she looked at the list, she felt like someone steering again.

qa.q: How many items were on Keerthana's list?
qa.a: The list had eleven items.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana feel like "someone steering again" on day nine?
qa.a: Doing tasks one by one gave her proof she could act, even though the fear remained. The threat was still big, but it no longer felt like a wall she couldn't touch.

qa.q: Which question from Sahil helped Keerthana start, and why?
qa.a: "Which one takes under an hour?" It made the first step small enough to do that same night.

qa.q: How might Sahil have felt watching Keerthana on day three?
qa.a: Sahil was probably worried to see Keerthana so shaken, and wanted to be useful rather than just comforting. Bringing idli and a notepad shows a choice of practical help.

grounding: A young woman facing a layoff lists tasks, does the smallest one first, and regains a sense of control over days.

subtype: Problem solving one piece at a time [Response]
passage: Madhav, you look like I did in 2009. Sit, have some of this tea. I'm Shankar, and I was a young man of twenty-five that year when the textile mill closed. Four hundred of us got a letter on a Monday. I went home and told your aunty nothing. I just lay on the bed looking at the fan. Everything felt too big: my sister's school fees, the loan, the baby on the way. On Thursday my old supervisor came by and said, "Shankar, don't think about the whole mountain. What's one thing you can do before lunch?" I said I could go to the labour office and get my settlement papers. So I went. After lunch, I wrote one letter to a dyeing unit in Erode. That's all. The next day, one more thing. It took five months to find this job, but I stopped staring at fans. So what's your one thing before lunch?

qa.q: How many workers got a letter when the textile mill closed?
qa.a: Four hundred workers got a letter on a Monday.

qa.q: Why did Shankar lie on the bed looking at the fan?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed by everything at once, his sister's fees, the loan and the baby on the way, and did not know where to begin.

qa.q: What turning point did Shankar's supervisor create, and what did Shankar do with it?
qa.a: The supervisor asked for one thing Shankar could do before lunch. Shankar went for his settlement papers and then wrote one letter, which started a daily habit of small steps.

qa.q: What might Madhav be feeling when Shankar ends with "what's your one thing before lunch?"
qa.a: Madhav may feel put on the spot but also less alone, since someone older has been through the same fear and come out of it.

grounding: An older man tells Madhav how, after losing his job, he took one small task at a time until he found work.

subtype: Problem solving one piece at a time [Response]
passage: Deepak got the layoff call on the same day the power went out across his street. No Wi-Fi, a phone at 18 percent, and a flat that grew darker by the minute. Panic climbed: rent, the course fees, what would his parents say? His flatmate Mahima found him pacing with the torch. "Sit. Write it down while there's light." On the back of an old electricity bill Deepak scribbled a list: notice pay, CV, references, tell parents, budget. "Pick one you can do with no internet," Mahima said. He could draft the message to his parents on paper. He did, crossing out twice. When the power came back at nine, he sent it and charged his phone. His father replied, "We're with you, beta." Deepak circled "CV" for tomorrow morning and slept better than he expected.

qa.q: What did Deepak write his list on?
qa.a: On the back of an old electricity bill.

qa.q: What was Deepak worried about as the panic climbed?
qa.a: He worried about rent, his course fees and what his parents would say about the layoff.

qa.q: In the power cut, what choice helped Deepak move from pacing to acting?
qa.a: Picking a task he could do without internet: drafting the message to his parents on paper. Doing one thing broke the panic.

qa.q: How might Deepak's father have felt receiving the message?
qa.a: He was likely sad for his son but glad Deepak told them quickly and clearly. His reply "We're with you, beta" shows he wanted him to feel supported.

grounding: A young man who loses his job during a power cut writes a task list and completes one step he can manage, which calms him.

passage: Chaitanya's grandmother died two days before Diwali, and the house that had been full of lamps was suddenly full of relatives and quiet. There was no time to grieve: the rituals needed arranging, the priest was double-booked, and it was pouring. His cousin Lalit arrived soaked, holding marigolds. Together they washed the courtyard for the thirteenth-day prayers. Chaitanya kept expecting to hear her calling him to taste the laddoos. During the chanting he cried, and so did Lalit. Afterwards the neighbours came with food, each telling a small story about her: the extra rotis she sent over, the sari she stitched for a bride. Chaitanya listened and felt something loosen. "It still hurts," he said to Lalit that night. "But I feel like she's everywhere in this street." Lalit nodded. "She is."

qa.q: When did Chaitanya's grandmother die?
qa.a: She died two days before Diwali.

qa.q: Why did the neighbours' stories make Chaitanya feel something loosen?
qa.a: Hearing how his grandmother helped others showed that her life still mattered to many people. That shared memory made the grief easier to hold, even though it still hurt.

qa.q: At the prayers, Chaitanya let himself cry instead of holding it in. How did that choice help him through the day?
qa.a: Crying alongside Lalit during the chanting let the grief be shared rather than hidden. Afterwards he was open enough to take comfort from the neighbours.

qa.q: How might Lalit have felt arriving soaked with marigolds in the rain?
qa.a: Lalit was grieving too, and helping with the rituals was a way to show love for the grandmother and support Chaitanya. 🤍

grounding: A young man grieving his grandmother finds comfort in the rituals and in the neighbours' stories about her, though it still hurts.

passage: Every Sunday morning since her husband's accident, Nikita had taken the 8 a.m. metro to the community kitchen near Chandni Chowk. She was twenty-five and a widow of eight months. At first she went because her friend Gautam dragged her. Now she went without being asked. She chopped onions next to strangers, stirred huge pots of rajma and handed plates to labourers and old men. Some weeks she still cried on the metro back. One Sunday an elderly man took his plate, looked at her and said, "God bless your hands, beti." Nikita smiled and felt, for a moment, that her grief had somewhere to go. Gautam, drying steel plates, caught her eye. "You okay?" "No," she said honestly. "But this helps. It doesn't make sense of it. It just makes it... carryable."

qa.q: How long had Nikita been a widow?
qa.a: She was a widow of eight months.

qa.q: What did Nikita mean when she called her grief "carryable"?
qa.a: Helping others did not explain or remove the loss, but it gave her pain some purpose and made it possible to live with.

qa.q: At first Gautam dragged Nikita to the kitchen. What changed when she started going on her own?
qa.a: It became her own choice and source of meaning, not just a friend's idea. That is when the work began to comfort her.

qa.q: How might the elderly man's blessing have affected Nikita?
qa.a: It made her feel useful and seen at a time when she felt broken. For a moment, her grief had somewhere to go.

grounding: A young widow finds her grief more bearable through serving food at a community kitchen, though it does not make sense of her loss.

passage:
"Naveen, you haven't touched Appa's chair in a month."
"I can't, Suraj. It still smells like him."
"Amma asked if we'd come to the temple with her tomorrow. It's the monthly puja."
"I don't even know if I believe in any of that."
"Me neither, fully. But Amma does. And Appa loved the drive."
Next morning the brothers sat on the cold temple floor with their mother. The bells rang. Naveen found himself saying the words Appa used to mumble.
In the car he said, "I thought it'd make it worse."
"Did it?"
"No. It felt like doing something with him instead of just missing him."
Suraj squeezed his shoulder. "Next month too?"
"Next month too."
That evening Naveen sat in Appa's chair for the first time.

qa.q: What was the occasion at the temple?
qa.a: It was the monthly puja.

qa.q: Why was Naveen unsure about going to the temple?
qa.a: He was not sure he believed in the rituals and feared it would make his grief worse.

qa.q: Naveen chose to go despite his doubts. Why did that choice matter?
qa.a: Joining the ritual with his family let him feel connected to Appa instead of only missing him, and that evening he could finally sit in his father's chair.

qa.q: How might Amma feel seeing both sons with her at the puja?
qa.a: She probably felt comforted and less alone in her grief, sharing something that meant a lot to her and to their father.

grounding: Two brothers grieving their father find comfort in a monthly temple ritual with their mother, even without full faith.

subtype: Recognising the limit and asking for help [Response]
passage: Yosef had been sleeping four hours a night since he took over his father's bakery in Haifa. Orders were late, he'd shouted at a supplier, and last Tuesday he'd sat in the cold store for twenty minutes because he couldn't face the counter. On Friday evening, washing trays, he said to his sister Noa, "I'm not managing. It's not just tired." Noa turned off the tap. "Thank you for saying it." That weekend he told his mother and uncle too, and they worked out who could cover mornings. On Monday he booked an appointment with a psychologist a friend had recommended. He felt embarrassed in the waiting room. But when he came out, he texted Noa: "Next appointment's Thursday. I think I did something right." She sent back a heart.

qa.q: Where did Yosef sit for twenty minutes last Tuesday?
qa.a: He sat in the cold store because he couldn't face the counter.

qa.q: How did Yosef feel in the waiting room, and why?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, perhaps because asking for professional help felt like admitting weakness after trying to cope alone.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Yosef, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Telling Noa "I'm not managing" while washing trays. It led to telling his family, sharing the mornings and booking a psychologist.

qa.q: How might Noa have felt when Yosef texted after his first appointment?
qa.a: She was probably relieved and proud of her brother, since his words showed he felt he had done something right.

grounding: A young man running a bakery abroad tells his family he is not coping and books a psychologist, feeling he did something right.

subtype: Recognising the limit and asking for help [Response]
passage: Minakshi had been a nurse on the children's ward for three years, and lately she was crying in the staff toilet between rounds. She snapped at a parent on Monday and forgot a chart on Wednesday. On Thursday, after handover, her senior Bhavna found her in the break room staring at cold tea. "You're not yourself." Minakshi started to say "just busy," then stopped. "I'm not coping. I can't sleep. I think I need help." Bhavna nodded. "The hospital has a staff counselling service. I'll cover your first appointment slot." That evening Minakshi called her mother and told her too. The next week she sat in the counsellor's office, hands clenched. "I thought asking would make me look weak," she admitted. The counsellor smiled. "It shows you know your limits. That's a strength."

qa.q: How long had Minakshi been a nurse on the children's ward?
qa.a: Three years.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi's hands clench in the counsellor's office?
qa.a: She was anxious, worried that asking for help would make her look weak.

qa.q: What choice did Minakshi make in the break room, and what did it set in motion?
qa.a: She chose to say "I'm not coping" instead of "just busy." That led to Bhavna covering her appointment slot, telling her mother, and starting counselling.

qa.q: How might Bhavna see Minakshi's honesty?
qa.a: Bhavna likely respects it and feels relieved, because a nurse who admits struggling can get help before mistakes grow. It also lets Bhavna support Minakshi as a senior.

grounding: A nurse who realises she is not coping tells her senior and her mother and goes to the staff counsellor, learning it is a strength.

subtype: Recognising the limit and asking for help [Response]
passage:
Tarun,
I'm writing this because saying it on the phone felt too hard. I haven't been okay for a while. Since the promotion I've been working till midnight, and I've stopped enjoying anything. Last week I cried in the office parking lot and couldn't stop. I kept thinking I just needed to push harder.
I've realised I can't fix this alone. I've made an appointment with a counsellor for Saturday. I'm scared, and a bit ashamed, if I'm honest. You've always been the strong one.
Could you call me after the session? I'd like you to know how it goes. And please tell Maa gently; I'll talk to her myself on Sunday.
Thank you for always picking up.
Your brother,
Nilesh

qa.q: When is Nilesh's appointment with the counsellor?
qa.a: It is on Saturday.

qa.q: Why does Nilesh feel "a bit ashamed" about seeing a counsellor?
qa.a: He had believed he should just push harder, and compares himself with Tarun, "the strong one." Admitting he can't fix things alone feels like a failure at first.

qa.q: What choice did Nilesh make after crying in the parking lot, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He stopped trying to push harder and booked a counsellor, then told Tarun. Reaching for professional help and family is the step that can actually change things.

qa.q: How might Tarun feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Tarun is likely worried for Nilesh but touched to be trusted with this. Tarun may also feel responsible to call after the session and be gentle with Maa.

grounding: A young man writes to Tarun that he is not coping, has booked a counsellor, and asks for his family's support.
